This is one of the most common medications implicated in toxic optic neuropathy. Optic neuropathy resulting from toxic exposure is characterized by a gradual, progressive, and painless vision loss. Visual ﬁelds typically show either bilateral central or cecocentral scotomas. An arcuate scotoma is a nerve ﬁber bundle defect typical of glaucoma. Homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing can be seen with optic tract, optic radiation, and occipital lobe lesions. Enlarged blind spots are classically seen with papilledema.

question: A 33-year-old man had sudden, complete, painless vision loss in his left eye that lasted 10 to 15 minutes, before remitting completely. On examination, his visual acuity, perimetry, and fundus appearance are normal. The right pupil is 1 mm larger than the left and dilates more quickly in darkness. There is no relative aﬀerent pupillary defect. The left eyelid has 2 mm ptosis. What environmental insult might be elicited on further questioning?
explanation: This patient has physiologic anisocoria with <1mm anisocoria, with the same pupil disparity between bright and dim lighting conditions. Despite mild ptosis, the normal motility and levator function, along with the brisk pupillary light reactions, strongly suggest that the anisocoria is not due to a cranial nerve III (CN III) palsy. The ptosis is on the side of the larger (right) pupil, so the ﬁndings are not consistent with Horner syndrome. Absent evidence for an urgent process, imaging and/or hospitalization are not indicated at this time.

question: A 75-year-old woman presents for a routine examination. In bright light her pupils measure 3.5 mm OD and 3 mm OS, and in dim light they measure 5 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS. Both pupils are briskly reactive to light. She has 1 mm ptosis OD, normal levator function, and normal ocular motility. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: A restrictive process produces a mechanical limitation of the range of eye movements that can often be felt by the examiner when forceps or a cotton swab is used to advance the limited eye movements. To perform a forced duction test, topical proparacaine drops are applied to the eye and held over the limbal region with a cotton tip for 1 to 2 minutes. Then the conjunctiva at the limbus is grasped with toothed forceps, and the globe is passively rotated in the direction of limited abduction to assess for restriction of eye movement. A positive forced duction test results when there is restriction to passive eye movement.

question: A 55-year-old man has diplopia at distance with esotropia worse on left gaze. What oﬃce test is most helpful in diﬀerentiating a restrictive from a paralytic strabismus as the cause of the double vision?
explanation: Alternate cover testing, rather than cover/uncover, will unmask any phoria but will not inform the examiner about muscle function. Monocular occlusion is useful when the examiner suspects strabismus in a patient with no manifest deviation, as it breaks fusion and can unmask a latent strabismus. Orbital cooling has been suggested in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis but cannot distinguish other paretic causes (such as 6th nerve palsy) from a restrictive process.

question: The classic triad of spasmus nutans includes ocular oscillations, head nodding, and what other symptom?
explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is a disease in which 90% of patients are women who are obese, and it peaks in the third decade of life. It presents with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. Common symptoms include headaches that are worse when lying down, transient visual obscurations, and pulsatile tinnitus. Visual ﬁeld testing, along with acuity and color testing, are mandatory to evaluate visual status and determine further treatment. MRI/MRV and lumbar puncture are used to rule out other causes of increased intracranial pressure such as a mass, dural sinus thrombosis, or meningitis. Poor visual prognosis is associated with male gender, African American race, morbid obesity (a BMI of 40 or more), anemia, and severe papilledema.

question: A 24-year-old obese white woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 41 presents with a few seconds of vision blurring with spontaneous recovery, headache, and a swooshing sound in her ears. She is found to have mild papilledema and a normal magnetic resonance imaging/magnetic resonance venography (MRI/MRV) result. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 45 cm of water. What features of her presentation are associated with poor prognosis?
explanation: In a 55-year old man, the most common cause of acute painless vision loss upon awakening is nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), especially in the setting of vascular risk factors. NAION is associated with the following risk factors: structural crowding of the disc (disc-at-risk), systemic hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, and BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 55-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obstructive sleep apnea awoke with painless vision loss in his left eye. He had no vision changes in the right eye. Examination showed hyperemic disc edema and peripapillary hemorrhages in the left eye. What nerve appearance would be expected in the right eye?
explanation: The anterior occipital lobe subserves the far temporal visual ﬁeld of the contralateral eye. In patients with anterior occipital lobe stroke involving the parieto-occipital artery, the resulting contralateral visual ﬁeld defect is crescent-shaped and starts about 60 degrees temporal of ﬁxation. Of the above choices, only Goldmann kinetic perimetry tests the outer edge of peripheral vision: temporally to 90 degrees; superiorly, inferiorly, and nasally to 60 degrees. Using several isopters (lights of standardized size and brightness), one can map a far temporal defect that would be missed on central vision testing. Tangent screen testing is another type of kinetic perimetry wherein the patient is tested with a stimulus at 1 m. The areas of patient response are marked and the patient is moved back to 2 m. The test is then repeated using an 18-mm white stimulus. It is most useful in revealing "tubular" ﬁeld defects typical of nonorganic visual loss and is not the ﬁrst-choice option for stroke detection. Frequency doubling threshold (FDT) perimetry is usually used as a screening test of the central 20-30 degree visual ﬁeld and would not be adequate to pick up defects in the far periphery. Computerized microperimetry with scanning laser ophthalmoscope (SLO) guidance tests the central macular visual ﬁeld by allowing the real-time functional study of retinal sensitivity by direct ophthalmoscopy of the retinal surface at each test location. It is an appropriate method for analyzing central visual ﬁeld defects but will miss peripheral depression outside 10-15 degrees.

question: Eight days ago, a 63-year-old woman had a right-sided anterior occipital stroke. She reports being startled by people coming from behind her on the left. She is slow to detect ﬁngers in her left peripheral visual ﬁeld but has normal standard automated perimetry. What test will best deﬁne the suspected ﬁeld defect? &
explanation: Although this patient ﬁts the demographics for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion only after neuroimaging and lumbar puncture have been performed to rule out another underlying cause. Neuroimaging should be performed before a lumbar puncture because it may provide an obvious cause of the elevated intracranial pressure and alleviate the need for a lumbar puncture. Also, it is important to rule out a large mass or BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 23-year-old obese woman with a recent 10-pound weight gain presents with a headache and is found to have bilateral optic disc swelling. What is the most appropriate next step? &
explanation: Several neuro-ophthalmic abnormalities occur with greater frequency or can be exacerbated during pregnancy or the postpartum period. These disorders include cerebral venous thrombosis, pituitary apoplexy, pseudotumor cerebri, and lymphocytic hypophysitis. Bitemporal hemianopia suggests damage to the optic chiasm from pituitary compression, commonly seen in the postpartum female with pituitary apoplexy. Hemorrhage within the tumor causes acute, painful ophthalmoplegia by extension into the adjacent cavernous sinus and is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment. Homonymous hemianopia in a postpartum woman could be suggestive of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). However, in this case, MRI would be expected to show T2-hyperintense vasogenic edema involving the white matter of the posterior cerebral regions. Arcuate visual ﬁeld defects and blind spot enlargement both could occur in the setting of papilledema associated with cerebral venous thrombosis or pseudotumor cerebri. While symptoms of headache, nausea, vomiting, and diplopia could be consistent with increased intracranial pressure, the MRI would not demonstrate a hemorrhagic pituitary lesion in these cases.

question: For 3 months, a 50-year-old woman has noticed decreased vision OS, which she discovered when covering the right eye while looking in a mirror. Visual acuity is 20/20 OD and 20/100 OS. Further evaluation of the left eye shows a central and inferior ﬁeld defect, a relative aﬀerent pupillary defect, and the fundus image as shown. Funduscopy was normal OD. What is her most likely diagnosis? &
explanation: Downbeat nystagmus is the most common form of central vestibular nystagmus. It results from lesions that produce defective vertical gaze holding, characterized by an upward drift, then correction with a downward saccade. Lesions that cause downbeat nystagmus compromise the vestibulocerebellum (including the nodulus, uvula, ﬂocculus, and paraﬂocculus) and decrease the tonic output from the posterior semicircular canals to the ocular motor neurons. According to Alexander's law, the downbeating movements are accentuated in downgaze. Patients usually report oscillopsia. If there is a structural lesion causing the downbeat nystagmus, then it most commonly is located at the cervicomedullary junction. The most common causative lesion is a Arnold-Chiari I malformation, a developmental abnormality characterized by posterior fossa crowding and cerebellar tonsillar protrusion into the foramen magnum. A lesion of the dorsal midbrain may produce a Parinaud syndrome, characterized by upgaze palsy, convergence- retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation, eyelid retraction, skew deviation, disruption of convergence, and increase square-wave jerks. A lesion of the sella may produce a bitemporal hemianopia secondary to chiasmal compression and, rarely, a see-saw nystagmus. A lesion of the lateral medulla may produce a Wallenberg syndrome, characterized by ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation, contralateral loss of body pain and temperature sensation, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral ﬁrst-order Horner syndrome, and ipsilateral ocular tilt reaction.

explanation: The patient has characteristic ﬁndings for ocular neuromyotonia, with sustained inferior rectus contraction for 30-60 seconds after downgaze and return to primary gaze (from reading position to primary). The most common cause of ocular neuromyotonia is prior skull base radiotherapy with presumed damage to the aﬀected cranial nerve (CN III in this case). Ocular neuromyotonia may aﬀect any of the ocular motor nerves or their divisions. Botulinum toxin does not cause this condition. First-generation antipsychotic use may cause tardive dyskinesia, which can involve facial spasms but is not known to produce ocular neuromyotonia. Microvascular decompression is a treatment option for patients with hemifacial spasm. It does not cause ocular neuromyotonia. Patients may be treated with antiepileptic agents such as carbamazepine if symptoms are bothersome.

question: A 34-year-old woman in her 34th week of pregnancy develops pre-eclampsia. She is monitored successfully until she presents to the emergency department with acute-onset headache, altered mental status, and complete vision loss in both eyes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows increased ﬂuid- attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) signal in the bilateral occipital lobes. After she is stabilized, how should the ophthalmologist counsel her family regarding her visual prognosis? &

options.B: gadolinium enhancement of both optic nerves
options.C: non-enhancing tumor compressing the optic chiasm
options.D: periventricular white-matter lesions on ﬂuid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences

explanation: This patient initially presented with a right optic neuritis and later was shown to have an abnormal visual evoked potential (VEP) in both eyes. Abnormalities on VEP testing may indicate optic nerve dysfunction and can suggest an etiology. The most common wave measured in VEP testing is the P100 wave. Reduced amplitudes are less speciﬁc than is delayed P100 latency, which typically is seen with demyelinating optic neuropathies. Based on the history of optic neuritis and the evidence of bilateral optic nerve demyelination based on VEP, there is concern for multiple sclerosis. Therefore, central nervous system (CNS) white-matter lesions may be present as well. Asymptomatic demyelination, as may be present in this patient, can be diagnosed when the P100 latency is severely delayed.

question: A 31-year-old woman had subacute painful vision loss to counting ﬁngers in the right eye that recovered over the subsequent 3 months. One year later, visual acuity is 20/30 OD, 20/20 OS with a trace right relative aﬀerent pupillary defect and minimal right optic disc pallor. Visual evoked potential test results show markedly delayed P100 latency in both eyes. What abnormality is most likely present on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain?

options.A: gram-positive cocci in clusters, resistant to methicillin

explanation: A biopsy demonstrating nonseptate fungal hyphae would indicate rhinocerebral mucormycosis, which typically occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus or in immunocompromised patients. The initial infection spreads from the facial skin, nasal mucosa, paranasal sinuses, or hard palate. The fungus spreads to the nearby blood vessels, aﬀecting the orbital vessels, carotid arteries, cavernous sinuses, or jugular veins. Orbital and neurologic signs are produced by infarction, thrombosis, or hemorrhage. Untreated, rhinocerebral mucorrmycosis can lead to rapid deterioration, resulting in death within days. This patient has vision loss and ophthalmoplegia, indicating an orbital apex syndrome. Patients with orbital apex syndrome from mucorrmycosis have nearly a 100% chance of permanent vision loss and > 60% mortality rate, despite aggressive surgical debridement and administration of antifungal agents. Gram-positive cocci in clusters, resistant to methicillin, indicating methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), atypical mycobacterial infection, and granulomatous lesions with noncaseating centers, such as sarcoidosis, carry some risk of mortality and morbidity, but not to the extent of rhinocerebral mucormycosis. second decade.

explanation: Optic pathway glioma is a slow-growing tumor that typically aﬀects children. Ten to seventy percent (10%-70%) of patients have associated NF1, and those patients have a better prognosis. Patients with optic pathway gliomas most frequently present in the ﬁrst decade of life. Malignant gliomas (glioblastoma) are rare; they almost always occur in adult males, and they have a very poor prognosis, including almost certain death within 1 year. Optic pathway gliomas constitute about 1% of all intracranial tumors.

explanation: This case describes a patient with a left gaze palsy, as indicated by the compensatory left head turn. Many of these patients do not have diplopia because the sixth nerve nucleus contains 2 populations of motoneurons: (1) those that innervate the ipsilateral lateral rectus, and (2) those that travel via the medial longitudinal fasciculus to innervate the contralateral medial rectus. In addition, the mouth droop indicates facial palsy from 7th nerve fascicle ﬁbers that wrap around the 6th nerve nucleus prior to exiting the pons. Other diagnoses such as myasthenia gravis and the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome can present with a variety of motility complaints and facial weakness, but an ischemic lesion of the pons in this 70-year-old vasculopathic man is most likely. explanation: This patient has visible optic disc drusen OU. These calcium and hyaline deposits are often seen as hyperechoic lesions at the optic nerve head on B-scan ultrasonography. They may also be visualized with fundus autoﬂuorescence or on computed tomography (CT) scans. Nerve ﬁber bundle visual ﬁeld defects, worse inferonasally, are the most common type of visual ﬁeld defects seen with optic disc drusen but are not diagnostic. Although the calcium in optic disc drusen may be visible on CT scan, it is poorly imaged by MRI and might not be detected. Intracranial hypertension is associated with papilledema but is not an expected diagnosis in this patient.

question: The lacrimal pump system is driven by what nerve?
explanation: The lacrimal pump is driven by the action of the pretarsal orbicular oculi muscle, which is innervated by the facial nerve, or CN VII. CN III is the oculomotor nerve that supplies the medial, superior, and inferior rectus and oblique muscles, as well as the levator muscle. CN V is the trigeminal nerve; it supplies sensory innervation to the face as well as motor innervation to some muscles of mastication. CN VI innervates the abducens nerve.

explanation: Most cases of optic neuritis are either isolated or due to a demyelinating disorder. Common features of isolated optic neuritis include young age (mean 32 years) and female sex (77%), with subacute monocular visual loss that occurs over several days. Ninety-two percent of patients complain of pain with eye movements, and 65% of cases have only retrobulbar involvement. In typical optic neuritis, most patients experience improvement of vision within 1 month and recover the majority of their vision within 1 to 3 months of onset. Atypical features that should prompt further workup include older age, lack of pain, peripapillary hemorrhages, ocular inﬂammation such as uveitis, choroiditis, retinal changes, involvement of other cranial nerves, and lack of any improvement in vision after 1 month.

explanation: Anterior optic tract lesions from tumor compression or stroke create a homonymous hemianopia and may be accompanied by a RAPD contralateral to the lesion (ie, on the same side as the hemianopia). The RAPD occurs because the lesion aﬀects more ﬁbers from the contralateral optic nerve. About 53% of ﬁbers from each optic nerve cross at the chiasm, and this asymmetry is enough to cause a mild RAPD with a tract lesion. Although improper technique can lead the examiner to a false conclusion regarding the presence or absence of an RAPD, that is not the cause here.

question: A person presents with ptosis and horizontal gaze palsy associated with ataxia and areﬂexia. What is the diagnosis?

explanation: Transient monocular vision loss (TMVL) may herald cerebrovascular disease, usually of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery, that can place the patient at risk for hemispheric stroke. Data from the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) suggested that TMVL was less likely to result in stroke than other types of transient ischemic attacks (TIA). More recent data suggest that patients with TMVL should be evaluated with urgent brain MRI to look for diﬀuse- weighted imaging (DWI) abnormalities, as their presence indicates that cerebral ischemia has occurred recently. Such patients may be at high risk for stroke, and they may beneﬁt from rapid surgical treatment of vascular disease. Having such patients seen in a hospital stroke unit is the most eﬀective way to ensure they receive immediate evaluation. Giant cell arteritis must be considered as a cause of TMVL as well, but in this patient, the normal ESR and CRP, along with absence of symptoms, as well as the DWI abnormality, indicates that she needs stroke evaluation. Scheduling routine carotid ultrasonography or simply prescribing aspirin is not adequate.

explanation: This patient has classic signs and symptoms of a direct carotid- cavernous sinus ﬁstula. High-ﬂow, direct ﬁstulas most commonly occur after severe head trauma and produce a cranial bruit. Carotid-cavernous sinus ﬁstulas often produce elevated intraocular pressure, proptosis, and arterialization of conjunctival vessels. Compression of cranial nerve VI (CN VI) by an enlarged inferior petrosal sinus that drains the ﬁstula can cause a sixth nerve palsy. Abnormal connections between the carotid artery or its branches and the cavernous sinus introduce high arterial pressures into the normally low-pressure venous circulation of the cavernous sinus. Such a high-pressure connection may reverse blood ﬂow within the superior ophthalmic vein, leading to an enlarged and dilated superior ophthalmic vein. The other vessels listed (vein of Galen, superior sagittal sinus, ophthalmic artery) would not be expected to be enlarged from a carotid-cavernous sinus ﬁstula.
